questions.q: Per Salesforce's own large-data-volume guidance, roughly what concentration of child records under a single parent is the point where data skew problems typically begin?
options: There is no documented threshold; it depends entirely on edition
More than 10,000 child records under one parent
More than 100,000 child records under one parent
More than 1,000 child records under one parent
questions.explain: Salesforce's large-data-volume guidance identifies more than 10,000 child records associated with the same parent record as the point where skew-related performance problems typically start to appear.

questions.q: A catch-all 'Unassigned' Account accumulates hundreds of thousands of child Contacts. Updating many of those Contacts concurrently starts failing. What's the mechanism causing the failures?
options: A storage limit being exceeded
The Contacts exceeding a per-object field limit
Repeated locking of the shared parent Account during concurrent child updates
Field-level security blocking the updates
questions.explain: Updating many children of the same account concentrates lock contention on that one parent record, so concurrent updates fail when a lock on the parent is already held.

questions.q: What is the standard mitigation when an ownership-skewed user or queue (owning a very large number of records) genuinely can't be avoided?
options: Give the skewed owner no role in the role hierarchy, removing them and their records from role-based sharing calculations
Delete the skewed owner's records periodically
Convert all of the owner's records into External Objects
Disable sharing rules org-wide
questions.explain: Removing the skewed owner from the role hierarchy (giving them no role) takes their records out of role-based sharing calculations, avoiding the expensive cascade that an owner or role change would otherwise trigger.

questions.q: Why is lookup skew generally harder to detect in advance than account or ownership skew?
options: Lookup fields are hidden from all reporting tools
Salesforce actively suppresses warnings about lookup skew
Lookup skew only affects sandboxes, not production orgs
There is no dedicated tool that flags it, and it often only surfaces as lock exceptions under concurrent automation and volume
questions.explain: Lookup skew has no dedicated detection tool and typically only becomes visible when high-volume automation and concurrent updates against a heavily-referenced lookup target collide, producing lock exceptions that aren't obviously connected to the cause.

questions.q: What do the mitigations for account skew, ownership skew, and lookup skew all have in common, per this lesson?
options: They all require purchasing additional storage
They all involve reducing concentration on a single record, or removing that record from the mechanisms that make concentration expensive
They all require disabling Apex triggers on the affected object
They all require migrating the object to a Big Object
questions.explain: All three skew mitigations share the same underlying shape: spread concentration across more records, or take the concentrated record out of the sharing/locking mechanisms that make that concentration costly.
